items.title: George Avakian interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 21, 1998
items.q: for bands like Count Basie, Jimmy Lunceford and goodness knows for many years Fletcher Henderson

ctx.x: To take this idea into a kind of a current aspect, this kind of racial divisions that happened, sometimes not from the musicians but from outside. What do you see is the racial outlook of jazz today?

Well the sad part about it is that there’s a great deal of division, and it continues in a fairly subtle way. I wish it weren’t so because there’s a lot of talk about how color doesn’t mean anything in jazz, but unfortunately it does and it has since well really I guess it started just before World War II, and there was a kind of a movement when the bop musicians started to establish themselves, to ostracize white musicians to the point where it got to be harder and harder for white musicians to find work. Now…

Savoy Ballroom began to bring in white bands. In any event, it has reached the point where today there are very, very fine white musicians who can’t really find work and that especially holds in Europe where there was always a feeling of the, what shall we say, the romance and I don’t know the word exactly, the glamour of the primitive black man and his primitive music. That’s the way the early jazz fans seemed to look at jazz. And once that got washed away and people realized well that’s an inaccurate…

items.title: Avakian George — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: The way that came about was that – of course I had gotten quite a few Ellington – well, I started to think about how the Ellington band grew out of – in my consciousness – out of my interest in Casa Loma and Benny Goodman and Fletcher Henderson.

ctx.x: Yes, it was. There was no separate category anywhere in the press and so on. There was almost no press, in fact. Down Beat was operating at the time. So was Metronome, which was an older magazine. But you had no things – no references to jazz or even really to pop music as a separate category in the ordinary day-to-day press. This really started to break open through Benny Goodman, because he became so popular so quickly. He was sort of a special phenomenon. People did not write articles about Bing Crosby, for…

Mann School for Boys. It’s just a mile-and-a-half away from here. I never thought I’d live up here, near the school, but I became very found of Riverdale when I went to Horace Mann. The way that came about was that – of course I had gotten quite a few Ellington – well, I started to think about how the Ellington band grew out of – in my consciousness – out of my interest in Casa Loma and Benny Goodman and Fletcher Henderson. But that’s something we’ll come back to later. The interview with Goodman came about,…
